ap_physics_1-f01.title: Crate pulled by a rope at an angle across a rough floor

stimulus.description: A crate of mass $m=8\text{ kg}$ is pulled across a rough horizontal floor by a rope that exerts a force of magnitude $T=40\text{ N}$ at an angle $\theta=30^\circ$ above the horizontal. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the crate and the floor is $\mu=0.25$. The crate speeds up as it slides.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: On the dot below, which represents the crate, draw and label the forces (not components) that act on the crate while it slides. Each force must be represented by a distinct arrow starting on the dot.
parts.model_answer: Four arrows from the dot: weight straight down, the normal force straight up, the rope force up and to the right at the angle $\theta$, and kinetic friction to the left. The normal force is shorter than the weight because the rope pulls partly upward.

rubric_rows.criterion: Draws and labels all four forces: weight (down), normal force (up), rope tension (up and to the right) and kinetic friction (left), with no extra force
common_errors: adds a force of motion
omits the normal force

rubric_rows.criterion: Directions are correct: the rope force at the angle above the horizontal toward the direction of motion and friction opposite to the motion
common_errors: draws friction in the direction of motion

rubric_rows.criterion: The normal force arrow is shorter than the weight arrow because the rope has an upward component
common_errors: draws the normal force equal to the weight

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the magnitude of the acceleration of the crate in terms of $m$, $T$, $\theta$, $\mu$, and fundamental constants.
parts.model_answer: Vertical: $N+T\sin\theta=mg$ so $N=mg-T\sin\theta$. Horizontal: $T\cos\theta-\mu N=ma$, so $a=\dfrac{T\cos\theta-\mu(mg-T\sin\theta)}{m}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Applies the vertical equilibrium condition to find the normal force: $N=mg-T\sin\theta$
required_elements: N = m g - T sin theta
common_errors: uses N = m g

rubric_rows.criterion: Writes Newton's second law along the floor: $T\cos\theta-\mu N=ma$
required_elements: T cos theta - mu N = m a
common_errors: uses the full tension in the horizontal equation

rubric_rows.criterion: Combines the equations to the correct expression for $a$
required_elements: (T cos theta - mu (m g - T sin theta))/m
common_errors: omits the upward component of the rope force from the normal force

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Calculate the magnitude of the acceleration of the crate for $m=8\text{ kg}$, $T=40\text{ N}$, $\theta=30^\circ$ and $\mu=0.25$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates the normal force (about 58 newtons) from the expression in part B
common_errors: uses mg as the normal force

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates an acceleration of about 2.51 with units of meters per second squared
common_errors: uses the weight as the normal force

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: The rope is raised so that the angle increases by $15^\circ$, while the tension stays the same and the crate keeps sliding. Does the magnitude of the kinetic friction force increase, decrease, or stay the same? Justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: The friction force decreases. A larger angle gives the rope a larger upward component $T\sin\theta$, which lowers the normal force $N=mg-T\sin\theta$, and $f=\mu N$ decreases.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the kinetic friction force decreases
common_errors: states that friction stays the same because the crate weighs the same

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies that the larger upward component of the rope force reduces the normal force, and friction is proportional to the normal force
common_errors: argues only that the horizontal component of the tension decreases

ap_physics_1-f02.title: A ball of mass $m=0.15\text{ kg}$ moving horizontally at speed $v_1=8\text{ m/s}$ hits a vertical wall and bounces straight back. A force sensor in the wall records the force that the wall exerts on the ball during the contact

stimulus.description: A ball of mass $m=0.15\text{ kg}$ moving horizontally at speed $v_1=8\text{ m/s}$ hits a vertical wall and bounces straight back. A force sensor in the wall records the force that the wall exerts on the ball during the contact.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: On the axes provided, sketch the force that the wall exerts on the ball as a function of time during the contact, using the three data points. Label the axes with quantities and units and label the key values.
parts.model_answer: A straight line from the origin up to $800\text{ N}$ at $5\text{ ms}$ and a straight line back down to zero at $13\text{ ms}$ (a triangle).

rubric_rows.criterion: Both axes are labeled with quantities and units and a scale is shown
common_errors: omits units

rubric_rows.criterion: Plots the three points $(0,0)$, $(5\text{ ms}, 800\text{ N})$ and $(13\text{ ms}, 0)$ accurately
Draws a straight line segment from the origin to the peak
common_errors: draws a curve through the peak

rubric_rows.criterion: Draws a straight line segment from the peak back down to zero force at the end of the contact
common_errors: ends the graph with a nonzero force

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Determine the magnitude of the impulse that the wall exerts on the ball. Show how you use your graph from part A.
parts.model_answer: The impulse is the area under the force-time graph: $J=\tfrac12(800)(0.0130)\approx 5.20\text{ N s}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies the impulse as the area under the force-time graph
required_elements: impulse is the area under the force-time graph
common_errors: uses the slope of the graph

rubric_rows.criterion: Uses the triangle area $\tfrac12F_{\max}\Delta t$ with the total contact time
common_errors: uses only the rising part of the graph

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates an impulse of about 5.20 with units of newton seconds (or kilogram meters per second)
common_errors: forgets to convert milliseconds to seconds

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Calculate the speed of the ball just after it leaves the wall. Show your work.
parts.model_answer: The ball reverses direction, so $J=m(v_2-(-v_1))=m(v_2+v_1)$ and $v_2=J/m-v_1=34.7-8\approx 26.7\text{ m/s}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Applies the impulse-momentum theorem with the velocity reversing sign: $J=m(v_2+v_1)$
common_errors: uses J = m(v2 - v1) without the sign change

rubric_rows.criterion: Solves for $v_2=J/m-v_1$
common_errors: adds the initial speed to J/m

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates a rebound speed of about 26.7 with units of meters per second
common_errors: uses the impulse as the final speed

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: Suppose the ball were instead made of clay and stuck to the wall without bouncing. Would the magnitude of the impulse that the wall exerts on the ball be greater than, less than, or equal to the impulse in this experiment? Justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: The impulse would be less. The impulse equals the change in momentum; a ball that stops changes its momentum by $mv_1=1.20\text{ N s}$, while the bouncing ball changes its momentum from $-mv_1$ to $+mv_2$, a larger change.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the impulse would be less
common_errors: states the impulse would be the same because the speed before contact is the same

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies that the change in momentum is smaller when the ball only stops than when it reverses direction
common_errors: argues only that clay is softer

student_thinking: Represent the contact force as a force-time graph
Use the area under the graph as the impulse
Apply the impulse-momentum theorem with the velocity changing sign

key_conditions.condition: the wall force is the net force on the ball along the line of motion and changes linearly with time
key_conditions.evidence: the stimulus gives the force at three times and says the ball bounces straight back

verification.independent_path: the impulse is recomputed by numerical integration of the piecewise-linear force and the rebound speed by a linear solve of the impulse-momentum equation

parts.label: A
accepted_answers: A straight line from the origin up to $1000\text{ N}$ at $5\text{ ms}$ and a straight line back down to zero at $11\text{ ms}$ (a triangle).

rubric_rows.criterion: Both axes are labeled with quantities and units and a scale is shown
Plots the three points $(0,0)$, $(5\text{ ms}, 1000\text{ N})$ and $(11\text{ ms}, 0)$ accurately
Draws a straight line segment from the origin to the peak
Draws a straight line segment from the peak back down to zero force at the end of the contact

parts.label: B
accepted_answers: The impulse is the area under the force-time graph: $J=\tfrac12(1000)(0.0110)\approx 5.50\text{ N s}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies the impulse as the area under the force-time graph
elements: impulse is the area under the force-time graph

rubric_rows.criterion: Uses the triangle area $\tfrac12F_{\max}\Delta t$ with the total contact time
Calculates an impulse of about 5.50 with units of newton seconds (or kilogram meters per second)

parts.label: C
accepted_answers: The ball reverses direction, so $J=m(v_2-(-v_1))=m(v_2+v_1)$ and $v_2=J/m-v_1=36.7-12\approx 24.7\text{ m/s}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Applies the impulse-momentum theorem with the velocity reversing sign: $J=m(v_2+v_1)$
Solves for $v_2=J/m-v_1$
Calculates a rebound speed of about 24.7 with units of meters per second

parts.label: D
accepted_answers: The impulse would be less. The impulse equals the change in momentum; a ball that stops changes its momentum by $mv_1=1.80\text{ N s}$, while the bouncing ball changes its momentum from $-mv_1$ to $+mv_2$, a larger change.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the impulse would be less
Justifies that the change in momentum is smaller when the ball only stops than when it reverses direction

ap_physics_1-f02.title: A ball of mass $m=0.2\text{ kg}$ moving horizontally at speed $v_1=8\text{ m/s}$ hits a vertical wall and bounces straight back. A force sensor in the wall records the force that the wall exerts on the ball during the contact

stimulus.description: A ball of mass $m=0.2\text{ kg}$ moving horizontally at speed $v_1=8\text{ m/s}$ hits a vertical wall and bounces straight back. A force sensor in the wall records the force that the wall exerts on the ball during the contact.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: On the axes provided, sketch the force that the wall exerts on the ball as a function of time during the contact, using the three data points. Label the axes with quantities and units and label the key values.
parts.model_answer: A straight line from the origin up to $1000\text{ N}$ at $5\text{ ms}$ and a straight line back down to zero at $11\text{ ms}$ (a triangle).

rubric_rows.criterion: Both axes are labeled with quantities and units and a scale is shown
common_errors: omits units

rubric_rows.criterion: Plots the three points $(0,0)$, $(5\text{ ms}, 1000\text{ N})$ and $(11\text{ ms}, 0)$ accurately
Draws a straight line segment from the origin to the peak
common_errors: draws a curve through the peak

rubric_rows.criterion: Draws a straight line segment from the peak back down to zero force at the end of the contact
common_errors: ends the graph with a nonzero force

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Determine the magnitude of the impulse that the wall exerts on the ball. Show how you use your graph from part A.
parts.model_answer: The impulse is the area under the force-time graph: $J=\tfrac12(1000)(0.0110)\approx 5.50\text{ N s}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies the impulse as the area under the force-time graph
required_elements: impulse is the area under the force-time graph
common_errors: uses the slope of the graph

rubric_rows.criterion: Uses the triangle area $\tfrac12F_{\max}\Delta t$ with the total contact time
common_errors: uses only the rising part of the graph

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates an impulse of about 5.50 with units of newton seconds (or kilogram meters per second)
common_errors: forgets to convert milliseconds to seconds

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Calculate the speed of the ball just after it leaves the wall. Show your work.
parts.model_answer: The ball reverses direction, so $J=m(v_2-(-v_1))=m(v_2+v_1)$ and $v_2=J/m-v_1=27.5-8\approx 19.5\text{ m/s}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Applies the impulse-momentum theorem with the velocity reversing sign: $J=m(v_2+v_1)$
common_errors: uses J = m(v2 - v1) without the sign change

rubric_rows.criterion: Solves for $v_2=J/m-v_1$
common_errors: adds the initial speed to J/m

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates a rebound speed of about 19.5 with units of meters per second
common_errors: uses the impulse as the final speed

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: Suppose the ball were instead made of clay and stuck to the wall without bouncing. Would the magnitude of the impulse that the wall exerts on the ball be greater than, less than, or equal to the impulse in this experiment? Justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: The impulse would be less. The impulse equals the change in momentum; a ball that stops changes its momentum by $mv_1=1.60\text{ N s}$, while the bouncing ball changes its momentum from $-mv_1$ to $+mv_2$, a larger change.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the impulse would be less
common_errors: states the impulse would be the same because the speed before contact is the same

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies that the change in momentum is smaller when the ball only stops than when it reverses direction
common_errors: argues only that clay is softer

ap_physics_1-f03.title: A student hangs a metal cylinder from a force sensor and lowers it into a tank of an unknown liquid. For each trial the student records the submerged volume $V$ of the cylinder and the force-sensor reading $W_{app}$ (the apparent weight), with the cylinder at rest

stimulus.description: A student hangs a metal cylinder from a force sensor and lowers it into a tank of an unknown liquid. For each trial the student records the submerged volume $V$ of the cylinder and the force-sensor reading $W_{app}$ (the apparent weight), with the cylinder at rest.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Describe an experimental procedure to collect the data for the apparent weight as a function of the submerged volume. Include the equipment and the measurements, how the independent variable is changed, and one way to reduce the uncertainty in a reading.
parts.model_answer: Hang a cylinder with marked volume divisions from a force sensor, lower it into the liquid until each successive marked division is at the surface, wait until it is at rest, and read the sensor; repeat each reading several times and average.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies the measured quantities and equipment: a force sensor (or scale) for the apparent weight and a way to know the submerged volume (marks on the cylinder or the liquid level)
required_elements: force sensor and a way to know the submerged volume
common_errors: omits how the submerged volume is known

rubric_rows.criterion: Changes only the submerged volume while keeping the same cylinder and liquid, and reads the sensor with the cylinder at rest (both conditions are needed)
required_elements: change only the submerged volume with the object at rest

rubric_rows.criterion: Reduces uncertainty by repeating each reading and averaging, or by waiting for the reading to settle (either earns the point)
required_elements: repeat and average or wait to settle (either earns the point)

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Using the relationship between the apparent weight, the weight in air, the density of the liquid and the submerged volume, identify the quantities that should be plotted on the vertical and horizontal axes so that the data produce a straight line whose slope can be used to find the density of the liquid.
parts.model_answer: Plot $W_{app}$ on the vertical axis against $V$ on the horizontal axis; $W_{app}=W-\rho gV$, so the slope is $-\rho g$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies $W_{app}$ (vertical) versus $V$ (horizontal)
common_errors: plots V versus W_app and uses the wrong slope relation

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: On a blank grid whose scale you choose, plot the data and draw a best-fit line. Label the axes with quantities and units and use a scale that fills most of the grid.

rubric_rows.criterion: Axes are labeled with quantities and units and the scale fills most of the grid
common_errors: scale uses less than half the grid

rubric_rows.criterion: Plots the five points accurately
Draws a straight best-fit line through the trend of the points
common_errors: connects the dots

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: Use the best-fit line to determine the density of the liquid. Show your work.
parts.model_answer: The slope is about $-0.0077\text{ N/cm}^3=$-7695\text{ N/m}^3$ in magnitude, so $\rho=|\text{slope}|/g\approx 785\text{ kg/m}^3$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates the slope of the best-fit line using two points on the line (about -0.0077 N/cm^3; accept any value within 5 percent) and converts to N/m^3
common_errors: uses data points rather than points on the line
forgets to convert cubic centimeters to cubic meters

rubric_rows.criterion: Relates the magnitude of the slope to the density: $|\text{slope}|=\rho g$
common_errors: uses slope = rho

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates the density (about 785; accept any value within 8 percent) with units of kilograms per cubic meter
alt_solutions: a density consistent with the student's own slope from D1, $\rho=|\text{slope}|/g$

ap_physics_1-f04.title: Claim about a dropped ball and a horizontally launched ball

stimulus.description: Two identical small balls are at the edge of a horizontal table of height $h=1\text{ m}$. At the same instant one ball is dropped from rest and the other is launched horizontally with speed $v_0=2\text{ m/s}$. Air resistance is negligible. A student claims that the ball that is launched horizontally takes longer to reach the floor because it travels farther.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Do you agree or disagree with the student's claim? Justify your answer qualitatively without calculating numbers.
parts.model_answer: Disagree. The horizontal and vertical motions are independent. Both balls start with zero vertical velocity and have the same vertical acceleration $g$ over the same height, so they reach the floor at the same time.

rubric_rows.criterion: Disagrees with the claim (the two balls land at the same time)
common_errors: agrees because the launched ball travels a longer path

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies that the vertical motion does not depend on the horizontal motion
required_elements: vertical and horizontal motions are independent
common_errors: argues only that gravity acts on both balls

rubric_rows.criterion: Notes that both balls have the same initial vertical velocity (zero), the same acceleration and the same height
required_elements: same initial vertical velocity, acceleration and height
